newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Volvo share seen dipping after redemption.
newsitem.headline: Volvo share seen dipping after redemption.

text.p: A redemption programme has fuelled a 16 percent surge in Swedish vehicle maker AB Volvo's share price since March, but analysts said on Friday some profit-takers may lurk when the buy-back ends.

However, because of strong sales figures for the first part of the year, a favourable mark/dollar exchange rate and a successful launch of its new car and truck models, the fall would not be dramatic.
"The general market view is that the redemption right is helping the share in the bull direction," one Stockholm broker said.
"Volvo has been firm while the rest of the capital goods sector has gone off. But valuation wise I have no problem buying the share at this price," the broker said.
Volvo announced in March that it would redeem one in every 20 shares, or a maximum of five percent of the total number, at 40 crowns above the market price.
The price, to be announced on June 9, will be calculated from the average of the three highest volume-weighted closing prices reached between May 13 and June 6 plus 40 crowns.
Swedish brokerage Afred Berg put the redemption price at 256 crowns on May 30.
"We have seen good volumes in the stock and focus might shift away," Gustaf von Essen, a Volvo analyst at Swedish brokerage Carnegie, told Reuters.
"I don't think there will be any dramatic fluctuations, but it might weaken," he said.
"During this period we see considerable support for the share for technical trade reasons, which may disappear when this period ends," one Stockholm-based options trader said.
"A lot depends on general developments of the market. It's very hard to give any magnitude but I certainly don't see any crash," the trader said.
Volvo's share has risen some 16 percent since the redemption programme details were unveiled, lifting the share to a record intra-day high of 219 crowns earlier this week.
Some brokers noted that other shares in the automotive sector such as Swedish truck and bus maker Scania had seen profit-taking lately, while the Volvo share held ground.

"We see more potential in Scania which we have an 'outperform' on compared to 'neutral' on Volvo. Scania is more exposed to the truck market in Europe, and we expect it to take off within a year," said Gunnar Andersson at Handelsbanken.

Volvo's car business was more uncertain because of strong competition, analysts said. The company itself said in April that it expected strong competition in 1997 and no favourable price developments.
Volvo said this week that its total new car registrations rose 16.2 percent to 129,445 vehicles in the first four months of the year and that its truck sales jumped 32 percent.

"The 32 percent increase in order intake for trucks in the first four months of the year compared with the same 1996 period is stronger than what the market had anticipated," said Swedbank analyst Mats Liss.
But some analysts pointed out weak figures in 1996 make this year's figures appear especially good.

"It's very much in line with expectations that order figures in the first half of the year are strong in order for the volumes to reach the figure that are generally expected for the full year for both cars and trucks," von Essen said.
"Remember that last year we phased out the 400 series and the S40 was not yet on the market. This year the S40 is in the market and at a nice speed," a Volvo spokesman told Reuters.
Dresdner Kleinwort Benson analyst Karl-Johan Bonnevier said several factors, including a weak mark, helped justify the Volvo share price surge.
"We see the share stable at these levels," said Bonnevier, who has a hold recommendation on the share.

"Volvo has strong inflows in U.S. dollars and large outflows in marks and currencies related to the mark...The company has a very close correlation in its trading to how the dollar-to-mark develops," he said.
